name: Executive Order of May 29, 1873 establishing the Mescalero Apache Reservation (taking of Mescalero aboriginal lands)
promises: This was an executive order, not a treaty. It set apart a reservation in south-central New Mexico for the Mescalero Apache; later executive orders enlarged it.
No payment was offered for the much larger Mescalero homeland between the Rio Grande and the southern and eastern lines of New Mexico that the reservation replaced.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission held that the Mescalero aboriginally used and occupied lands in New Mexico east of the Rio Grande, and that on May 29, 1873, the date of the executive order creating their reservation, the United States acquired their Indian title to those lands without payment of compensation. It ordered the land valued as of that date, excluding confirmed Spanish and Mexican grants.

landTaken: The Mescalero aboriginal lands described in the Commission's Finding No. 37, in New Mexico east of the Rio Grande and south of about the 35th parallel, less confirmed Spanish and Mexican grants (Docket 22-B, 1966). The acreage was not found in a source opened.
compensation: None at the time. Final judgment of $8,500,000 by compromise in 1967 (Docket 22-B).
today: The Mescalero Apache Tribe holds the Mescalero Apache Reservation in south-central New Mexico, the reservation this order began.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says the mountains, plains and deserts of the region belonged to the Mescalero long before settlers came, that its reservation, long recognized by Spanish, Mexican and American treaties, was formally set up by President Grant's Executive Order of May 29, 1873, and that today's 463,000 acres are only part of what was once the heartland of its aboriginal homelands.
